pages.title: The Visit
pages.content:
One hour, one lift

Note 01

Per lift

60 minutes

An inspection hour is sixty minutes for one lift, with two technicians, five stops and a 32-point checklist on paper. The written report follows in two working days.

Part
01

One hour,
three parts

Every inspection hour follows the same three parts. From minute 0 to minute 10 we arrive: we meet the building manager, sign in, stand the notice at the landing and take that lift out of service. From minute 10 to minute 50 we inspect. The two technicians work through five stops and mark a 32-point checklist on paper while the lift stays out. From minute 50 to minute 60 we report. The lift goes back into service, and we go through the findings with the manager on that same paper. The written report follows within two working days. A slot starts at 07:00 or at 18:00, Monday to Friday, so the hour sits outside the building's busy times. The next free slot is Tuesday at 07:00. One hour covers one lift. A second lift on the same visit is a second hour.

Part
02

Five stops,
thirty-two points

The stops run in visit order: the landing, the car, the pit, the machine and the lobby. Landing doors account for six points, the car for five, car doors for four, the pit for four, rails and guides for three, the machine for four, the controller for four, and the lobby and signs for two. That is the full thirty-two, and the hour is built to mark all of them. At the landing we look at the doors and the sill. In the car we look at the interior, the panel and the doors from inside. The pit is buffers, guide rails and the space under the car. The machine stop is the traction machine and the controller cabinet. The lobby stop is the notice, the signs and the landing as someone waiting would meet it. The checklist and the written report are included in the inspection hour.

Part
03

What we ask of
the building

We ask for a manager on site at the start and again for the last ten minutes, so the findings are heard by the person who runs the building. The lift needs to be free for the full sixty minutes, with the notice standing at the landing and a clear way to the pit and the machine room. Keys for those rooms should be ready at sign-in. The hour does not pause while someone looks for them. Where the building has more than one lift, the others can stay in service. At Meridian Yard, twelve floors and three lifts, manager Lucia Ferrante booked three separate sixty-minute slots across two mornings so a lift stayed free for early staff. We do not need the whole building closed. Office hours for arranging this are Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 17:00, at +1 555 0142 or book@noboru-lifts.example.

The 32 points

Eight groups, filled in on paper at the stop where each point belongs.

Landing doors

6

Car

5

Car doors

4

Pit

4

Rails and guides

3

Machine

4

Controller

4

Lobby and signs

2

Total

32

What happens if a
fault appears

A fault found during the hour is written on the checklist at the stop where it shows. The inspection does not turn into a repair. In the last ten minutes we walk the manager through the sheet, then return the lift to service. The written report sets the same points down within two working days. At Alder House, nine floors and two lifts, manager Priya Nair had a door that hesitated on floor 6. The hour traced it to a worn sill guide. The guide was named on the paper. It was not replaced during the visit. A door that needs adjustment is a separate door adjustment visit. A fault that needs a call-out is a separate visit, Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 19:00. Samira Haddad writes the report from the sheets the technicians bring back.

Book an inspection

pages.title: Buildings
pages.content:
Office buildings

Note 01

Buildings of

4–12 floors

Three office buildings show the work we book: four to twelve floors, a manager on site, and one quiet hour when a lift can come out of service.

Case
01

Alder House

Alder House is nine floors with two lifts. The manager is Priya Nair. One door hesitated on floor 6. During the inspection the two technicians worked the landing and the car doors, and the hesitation was traced to a worn sill guide. The point was marked with the other landing-door items on the paper checklist, then read again in the last ten minutes, when the lift went back into service. Priya stayed for that conversation and read the sheet with us. The written report followed within two working days and carried the same note. The second lift had its own hour on the same visit. Nine floors sits inside the four-to-twelve range we book. We did not replace the guide during the inspection. The visit recorded where the hesitation came from, on paper, so the manager could decide the next step with the sheet in hand.

Case
02

Foundry Court

Foundry Court is six floors and one lift, in a converted warehouse. The manager is Daniel Osei. The lift was old and had no paperwork, so the inspection hour became its first written record. Two technicians took the five stops in order: landing, car, pit, machine and lobby. All thirty-two points went onto the paper checklist, including the points that simply confirmed what was there. With no earlier sheets to set beside them, the record itself was the result of the hour. Daniel met us at sign-in and again for the last ten minutes, when the lift returned to service and we read the findings from the pages. Samira Haddad wrote the report, and it went out within two working days. Six floors and a single lift is the smaller end of the offices we schedule. The hour started a file. It did not invent a history the lift had never had.

Case
03

Meridian Yard

Meridian Yard is twelve floors with three lifts. The manager is Lucia Ferrante. Twelve floors is the top of the range we book, and three lifts cannot share one hour, so we inspected them one at a time across two mornings. That was three separate sixty-minute slots. Each slot was the full visit: two technicians, five stops and the 32-point checklist on paper. A lift stayed free for early staff because only one car was out at a time. Lucia chose the order of the lifts and was there to sign us in. Each hour ended the same way. The lift went back into service, the findings were read on paper, and the written report followed within two working days. The building did not close. The early slots started at 07:00, when the lobby was still quiet, which is the same start we offer every weekday.

Who a visit
does not suit

We book office buildings of four to twelve floors for facilities managers and owners. A building under four floors, or over twelve, sits outside the diary Elena Castellano keeps. The inspection hour is not a statutory examination, so a visit also does not suit anyone who needs a statutory certificate. The hour is the 32-point checklist, the conversation on paper, and a written report within two working days. A building that cannot free a lift for sixty minutes at 07:00 or at 18:00 has no start we can use. Those are the only two inspection starts, Monday to Friday. We do not shorten an hour to put several lifts into one slot. Each lift is its own sixty minutes. If the building falls outside this, the reply says so. A reply to a booking goes out within one working day.

Book an inspection

pages.title: Fees
pages.content:
Fees, in US dollars

Note 01

From

$240

Fees are in US dollars and exclude tax. The inspection hour includes the 32-point checklist and the written report.

Six fees

The price list has six items, in US dollars, excluding tax. An inspection hour for the first lift is $240. Each further lift on the same visit is $140. A door adjustment visit is $320. A monthly service agreement is $190 per lift per month. A fault call-out within call-out hours is $280. A written second opinion on a quote is $180. Call-out hours are Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 19:00. Inspection slots start at 07:00 or 18:00, Monday to Friday, and each slot is one hour for one lift. Office hours for booking and for questions about a line are Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 17:00. We do not convert these amounts into another currency. The next free inspection slot on the notice is Tuesday at 07:00. A booking is answered within one working day, from 14 Wharf Row, Easterhaven.

32-point checklist and written report included. All prices in USD, excluding tax. An inspection hour is not a statutory examination.

Fees

What is included

The inspection hour includes the 32-point paper checklist and the written report. The report is sent within two working days. Two technicians attend. The hour covers one lift and the five stops: landing, car, pit, machine and lobby. The groups on the sheet are landing doors (6), car (5), car doors (4), pit (4), rails and guides (3), machine (4), controller (4), and lobby and signs (2). A further lift on the same visit is charged at $140 and receives its own hour and its own checklist. A door adjustment, a fault call-out, a month of the service agreement and a second opinion on a quote are separate bookings at the prices above. They are not included in the $240. The monthly figure is $190 per lift. The agreement is its own line, booked on its own.

Is an inspection
hour a statutory
examination?

No. An inspection hour is not a statutory examination. It is sixty minutes with two technicians, five stops and a 32-point checklist on paper, followed by a written report in two working days. It does not stand in for an examination required by an authority, and the report is not a certificate. The same statement is in our terms. Booking the hour means booking that checklist and that report, at $240 for the first lift and $140 for each further lift on the same visit. Findings are discussed on the paper before we leave, in the last ten minutes, and then written up by Samira Haddad. If you need a statutory examination, say so when you book and we will tell you this visit is not that service. We would rather reply with a clear no within one working day.

How to read
an invoice

An invoice uses the same six names, in US dollars, excluding tax. The first inspection line is the first lift at $240. Any other lift seen on that same visit appears as its own line at $140. A door adjustment is its own line at $320, a call-out at $280, a second opinion at $180, and a month of the service agreement at $190 for each lift named. The checklist and the written report do not appear as extra lines on an inspection invoice. They belong to the inspection hour. Tax is outside these amounts. The invoice does not show a converted currency. If a line does not match one of the six items, ask before you pay it. Elena Castellano can point to the line. Call +1 555 0142 or write to book@noboru-lifts.example, Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 17:00.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
Since 2011

Note 01

The team

7 people

Noboru Lifts was founded in 2011 and works from 14 Wharf Row, Easterhaven. Seven people run the inspections, the reports and the diary.

Founded
2011

Founded in 2011

Ines Varga founded Noboru Lifts in 2011 and is the lead inspector. She still goes out on the hour. The company is seven people, working for facilities managers and owners of office buildings of four to twelve floors. The office is 14 Wharf Row, Easterhaven. You can reach it at +1 555 0142 or book@noboru-lifts.example, Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 17:00. The shape of the work has stayed the same since 2011. Two technicians, sixty minutes, five stops, a 32-point checklist on paper, and a written report within two working days. Slots start at 07:00 or at 18:00. A booking is answered within one working day. The next free slot is Tuesday at 07:00. Ines reads the difficult sheets herself. The size of the team is the size of the visit.

Why the
checklist is paper

The checklist stays on paper so the manager can see each point during the hour. Thirty-two points, in eight groups, are marked at the stop where they are looked at. In the last ten minutes we read those marks together at the desk, before a written report exists. The report follows within two working days and matches the sheets. Samira Haddad writes it from the paper the technicians bring back. Foundry Court had an old lift and no paperwork. The sheets from that hour became its first written record. We work the same way when a building already has a file. The new pages join what is there. The manager has already heard them, on the day, from the same paper. That conversation is minutes 50 to 60, after the lift is back in service.

Seven people

Ines Varga is founder and lead inspector. Kofi Mensah is senior technician for doors. Naledi Dube is senior technician for controllers. Arjun Menon is technician for machine rooms. Marek Lindqvist is technician for pits and rails. Samira Haddad is the report writer. Elena Castellano is office and scheduling. Two technicians attend each lift. Who they are depends on the stops that matter that day: doors with Kofi, controllers with Naledi, a machine room with Arjun, a pit with Marek. Ines joins when the building needs the lead inspector. Samira does not travel for the hour. She writes from the sheets, and the report leaves within two working days. Elena keeps the slots at 07:00 and 18:00, Monday to Friday, and replies to a booking within one working day.

Through the morning the hours run one lift at a time: sixty minutes, two technicians, five stops, the checklist on paper. Reports are written in the afternoon from those sheets. The second round starts at 18:00, the other time we take a lift out of service. Fault call-outs can still be answered until 19:00, Monday to Friday. When the office phone opens at 07:00, the first landing notice is already standing. Elena Castellano is who tells you which of those hours is still free. Early slots

Early slot

07:00, Mon–Fri

List

Join the list

The early slot starts at 07:00, Monday to Friday. Join the list if you want to hear when the next one of those hours is free.

Hear when a
07:00 slot opens

This list is only for the early inspection slot, the one that starts at 07:00, Monday to Friday. Leave your name, the building and an email. from you

We ask for the building name so we can tell whether it is an office of four to twelve floors, which is the range we schedule. A building outside that range receives a plain reply, not a place held on the list. One opening means one lift for sixty minutes, with two technicians. Further lifts each need their own hour. Office hours for a question about the list are Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 17:00, on +1 555 0142 or book@noboru-lifts.example, at 14 Wharf Row, Easterhaven. To leave the list, write to the same address and say so. Elena takes the email off. We do not pass the list to anyone else, and we do not add a name that did not ask. The day those early slots belong to starts at 06:30, with vans out by 06:40.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
Your details

This note says what we collect when you book a visit or join the early-slot list, and who at Wharf Row sees it.

What we collect
and who sees it

When you book an inspection we ask for your name, the building, the number of floors and an email address. When you join the 07:00 waiting list we ask for your name, the building and an email. If you call, the office diary takes the same kind of detail: who you are, which building, and how to reply. We use it to answer within one working day, to offer a slot at 07:00 or 18:00, and to send the written report after a visit. The report goes to the manager who met the technicians. We do not buy address lists, and we do not add you to the waiting list unless you asked. Elena Castellano handles scheduling. Samira Haddad sees the building name and the paper checklist when she writes. The technicians see the sheets for the hour they are on.

What we do
not publish

We do not publish your name, your email or your building's private details on the site. The accounts of Alder House, Foundry Court and Meridian Yard name Priya Nair, Daniel Osei and Lucia Ferrante because those are the visits we describe in public. They are not a client list for anyone else to reuse. Messages stay with the office at 14 Wharf Row, Easterhaven, because the diary and the reports are how the next visit is planned. To ask what we hold about you, or to correct a name or an email, write to book@noboru-lifts.example or call +1 555 0142, Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 17:00. We reply within one working day. To leave the early-slot list, say so in that message and Elena will take the email off. We do not state a retention period in years. We have no such figure.

pages.title: Terms
pages.content:
Terms

These terms cover an inspection hour booked with Noboru Lifts. Prices are in US dollars and exclude tax.

The hour you
are booking

An inspection hour is sixty minutes for one lift. Two technicians attend. They make five stops: the landing, the car, the pit, the machine and the lobby. They complete a 32-point checklist on paper. In the last ten minutes they return the lift to service and go through the findings with the manager. A written report follows within two working days. The first lift on a visit is $240. Each further lift on the same visit is $140 and has its own hour. Slots start at 07:00 or 18:00, Monday to Friday. Office hours are Monday to Friday, 07:00 to 17:00. We reply to a booking within one working day. The place of business is 14 Wharf Row, Easterhaven. Phone +1 555 0142. Email book@noboru-lifts.example.

An inspection hour
is not a statutory
examination

An inspection hour is not a statutory examination. Booking it does not produce a statutory certificate, and the written report is not one. The hour is the checklist and the conversation on paper, then the report Samira Haddad writes from those sheets. A fault noted during the hour is recorded. It is not repaired as part of the $240. A door adjustment visit is $320. A fault call-out within call-out hours, Monday to Friday 07:00 to 19:00, is $280. A monthly service agreement is $190 per lift per month. A written second opinion on a quote is $180. Those four are separate bookings. None of them is included merely because an inspection hour was booked. The checklist and the written report belong to the inspection hour and are not billed again.

Buildings, access
and invoices

We book office buildings of four to twelve floors. If the building falls outside that, we say so in the reply and we do not hold a slot. Each lift needs its own sixty minutes. We do not shorten the hour to fit several lifts into one morning. You are responsible for access to the landing, the pit and the machine room at the start, and for a manager who can hear the findings at the end. Fees are in US dollars and exclude tax. We do not quote a converted price. An invoice should show only lines from the six-item list. If you join the early-slot list, a message that a 07:00 hour has opened is an invitation to book, not a confirmed visit. The visit is confirmed when we reply to the booking. That reply is sent within one working day.

posts.title: What a paper checklist catches
posts.excerpt: Thirty-two points, marked on paper at five stops during a sixty-minute inspection, are what the written report is built from.
posts.content:
The inspection hour carries a paper checklist of thirty-two points. Two technicians mark it between minute ten and minute fifty, after the lift has been taken out of service and before it is returned. The points are grouped, and the groups always add up the same way: landing doors six, car five, car doors four, pit four, rails and guides three, machine four, controller four, lobby and signs two. The list is included in the hour. So is the written report that follows within two working days. Samira Haddad writes that report from the sheets. She does not invent a second list back at Wharf Row.

Landing doors are the first group, six points, and they are where a hesitation often shows. At Alder House, nine floors and two lifts, the manager Priya Nair had a door that hesitated on floor 6. The hour traced that hesitation to a worn sill guide. The finding went onto the paper at the landing, with the other door points beside it. It was still on the sheet at minute fifty, when we read the pages with Priya and then put the lift back into service. We did not change the guide during the inspection. The sheet named the part. The report, sent within two working days, named it again.

The car is five points and the car doors are four more. We keep them as separate groups because a door fault and a car fault are different work afterwards. Car doors sit with Kofi Mensah, the senior technician for doors. If a door later needs adjustment, that is its own visit at $320. It is not done inside the inspection hour, and it is not hidden inside the $240. At Alder House the worn sill guide stayed a landing-door finding. The hour recorded it. The adjustment, if Priya books one, is another morning.

The pit is four points. Rails and guides are three. Marek Lindqvist is the technician for pits and rails, and this part of the hour is his: buffers, guides, and the rails the car runs on, seen with a work light. The marks go on the same paper as the doors. A manager who never goes down to the pit still sees those lines at the desk in the last ten minutes. That is the reason the checklist is paper. The list has to be in the room with the person who will read it at minute fifty.

The machine is four points and the controller is four. Arjun Menon takes machine rooms. Naledi Dube takes controllers. The machine stop is the traction machine and the cabinet, looked at with the door open and left closed again before we go. Controller points sit next to machine points on the sheet, so a later quote can be read against a group. A written second opinion on someone else's quote is a different booking, at $180. The inspection list is only what these two technicians saw on the day, in that room, during that hour.

Lobby and signs are the last two points. They cover the landing as a person waiting would meet it, including the notice we stood there when we took the lift out of service. The notice comes down when the lift returns. The two points remain on the sheet. They are easy to treat as small, and we keep them, because the lobby is one of the five stops. Landing, car, pit, machine, lobby. Skip the last and the thirty-two are no longer complete.

When the papers are thin, the checklist is the whole record. Foundry Court is six floors and one lift, a converted warehouse, managed by Daniel Osei. The lift had no paperwork. The thirty-two points from that single hour became its first written record. Daniel heard them in the last ten minutes. Samira wrote them up within two working days. Where a building already has a file, the new sheets join it. We do not score the old file against the new one, and we do not publish a comparison.

The hour is not a statutory examination. The report does not certify the lift. A clear sheet is an account of one quiet hour, two technicians and thirty-two marks, not a promise about the weeks after we leave. The first lift is $240. Each further lift on the same visit is $140 and receives the same list, in its own sixty minutes. At Meridian Yard, Lucia Ferrante used three such hours across two mornings so twelve floors and three lifts could be checked with one car left free for early staff. That is what the paper catches. A named part, a full group count, and a page the manager has already seen before we leave the lobby.

posts.title: Why we start at seven
posts.excerpt: Early slots start at 07:00 because a lobby is quietest then, before the first tenants arrive.
posts.content:
Our first inspection slot of the day starts at 07:00. That is not a habit of the crew. A lobby at that hour is empty, the lifts are barely used, and a lift can be taken out of service for the hour without anyone waiting for it.

By the time the second technician has signed in at the desk, the landing doors have been opened and the paper checklist is out. The inspection takes one hour. The written report follows within two working days, and the building is back to normal before the first tenants walk in.

If 07:00 does not suit you, the other slot starts at 18:00, once the offices have emptied. Both run Monday to Friday, and both are the same hour.

posts.title: Reading an old lift’s logbook
posts.excerpt: The logbook kept in the machine room tells us as much about a lift as the lift does.
posts.content:
Most older lifts have a logbook kept in the machine room, a worn notebook with dates, initials and a line or two for each visit. We ask to read it before an inspection starts, and it often shapes the hour.

A repeated note about the same door tells us where to look first. A gap of several years tells us the checklist should be slower there. Entries are short, and the handwriting changes, but the pattern is usually clear in ten minutes.

After the visit we add our own line to the book, with the date and the report reference, so the next person who opens it finds the thread.
